title: Jobava London
sub: 1.d4 with Nc3 and Bf4: the system you already play as White
why: You play 1.d4, Nc3 and Bf4 in almost every White game, and the engine says you're usually better after 10 moves. But you only score 38% in these games. This course teaches the proper move order, the key tricks, and, most importantly, what to do once the opening is over.

lines.title: Black plays ...e6 and ...Bd6
lines.intro: The most common set-up. Black offers to trade bishops on d6. You'll get a grip on e5 and a clear plan.

moves.c: The Jobava move. The knight eyes b5 and e4, and together with Bf4 it creates threats against c7 very early.
Bishop out before e3, so it isn't shut in behind your pawns.

quiz.q: Why is Nb5 a good move here?
options: It attacks the d6 bishop and the c7 square, so Black must react at once
It prepares queenside castling
It protects the d4 pawn
quiz.explain: Nb5 hits d6 and eyes c7. If Black takes on f4, you take back with the e-pawn and control the e5 square.

moves.c: Take towards the centre. The f4 pawn now guards e5, a perfect square for your knight later.
Black kicks the knight.
Job done, back it goes. Black has no dark-squared bishop any more, so c5 and e5 are weak for Black.

quiz.q: Why take on c5 instead of developing with Bd3?
options: Black must spend a move winning the pawn back while you develop
It wins a pawn for good
It opens the d-file to attack d5
quiz.explain: Taking costs Black a tempo to regain the pawn and loosens Black's centre. The engine rates dxc5 as clearly best here.

moves.c: Plan from here: Qe2, Ne5 and Rae1. Your f4 pawn keeps e5 under control for your knight.

lines.title: Black pins with ...Bb4
lines.intro: Black pins your knight. Develop the other knight to e2 so that if Black takes on c3, you recapture with a piece and keep a healthy pawn structure.

quiz.q: Why the knight to e2 instead of f3?
options: So that after ...Bxc3 you can recapture with the knight and avoid doubled pawns
Because f3 is attacked by the bishop
To protect the queen
quiz.explain: From e2 the knight supports c3. If Black gives up the bishop on c3, Nxc3 keeps your pawns intact. One warning: don't rush Bd3 here. With your knight on e2 the bishop has no retreat, and ...c5-c4 can trap it.

moves.c: Ask the bishop a question.
Black keeps the bishop. After 6...Bxc3+ 7.Nxc3 you'd have the two bishops.
The knight heads for the kingside, eyeing h5 and f5.
Take when the bishop has to spend another move to recapture.
Now the bishop is safe: no c-pawn is left to trap it. Plan: O-O, e4 and a kingside attack with Nh5 or Qf3.

lines.title: Black develops ...Bf5
lines.intro: Black copies you with the London-style bishop. The simple plan: Nb5 and Nf3, then trade bishops. There's also a trick worth knowing.

moves.c: Straight at c7 again. Black has to cover it.
The knight on a6 is badly placed.
Kicks the knight.
Back to c3. Black has spent moves on ...Na6 and ...c6, and the a6 knight is out of play.
Offer the bishop trade.
Take with the pawn: it controls e4 and c4 and opens the c-file for your rook.
A mistake: the knight jumps forward, but it can simply be taken.

quiz.q: What should you check before worrying about ...Bxc3+?
options: Count material: after 10...Bxc3+ 11.bxc3 you are still a whole piece up
Your pawns will be doubled so you're worse
You must castle first
quiz.explain: If a knight jumps into your pawns, check whether you can simply take it. Always count what a threat really costs before panicking.

moves.c: White is a piece up. In real games Black usually plays 9...O-O instead, but now you know the trick.

lines.title: Black hits back with ...c5
lines.intro: The most active reply. Keep calm: e3 first. If Black then plays ...Nc6, your Nb5 comes with real threats against c7.

moves.c: Solid. Your d4 pawn is defended and the bishop is outside the pawn chain.
Natural, but it already allows a trick.
Threatening Nc7+, forking king and rook.

quiz.q: What is White's best reply to 5...e5?
options: dxe5, winning a pawn and keeping the c7 threat alive
Nc7+ at once
Bg3, keeping the bishop
quiz.explain: 6.dxe5 wins a pawn and the knight on f6 must move. Always look at captures first.

quiz.q: Why can White take on d5 even though Black's queen guards it?
options: Because after 7...Qxd5 8.Nc7+ the knight forks king and queen
Because the d5 pawn is pinned
Because Black's queen is trapped
quiz.explain: The fork on c7 is the whole point of Nb5. Look for knight forks whenever the king and a rook or queen stand on squares a knight can hit together.

moves.c: Block the check. White is two pawns up and still threatens Nc7+.

lines.title: Black exchanges with ...cxd4
lines.intro: The main line against ...c5. Take back with the e-pawn, open the e-file and develop fast.

moves.c: Take towards the centre. Your bishop on f4 is now outside a solid pawn chain.
Stops Nb5.
Ask the bishop: trade or retreat?
You get the bishop pair and the queen joins the game. Plan: Bd3, O-O and Re1.

lines.title: Black stops Nb5 with ...a6
lines.intro: Some players (like several of your opponents) play ...a6 early to stop Nb5. Then you develop, meet ...c5 by taking on c5, and grab the centre with e4.

moves.c: Stops Nb5 but uses a move.
Take on c5 when Black's bishop has to spend a move recapturing.

quiz.q: What does e4 achieve?
options: It frees your pieces and opens lines while Black's king is still in the centre
It wins the d5 pawn by force
It stops ...O-O
quiz.explain: With your lead in development, opening the centre with e4 is the right plan. If ...dxe4 then Nxe4 hits the c5 bishop with tempo.

lines.title: Black plays ...Nf6 and ...g6
lines.intro: Against the King's Indian set-up the engine likes a big centre with e4. You get the space; Black gets no easy targets.

moves.c: Your usual move. 3.e4 at once is even stronger and usually transposes.
Take the whole centre when Black allows it.
Plan: O-O-O, then Bh6 to trade Black's best bishop, and a pawn storm with f3, g4 and h4-h5.
Trade the Black king's defender.

quiz.q: What does f3 do?
options: It keeps Black's pieces out of e4 and g4 and prepares g4 and h4-h5
It defends against ...Qa5
It prepares Bf1-d3
quiz.explain: With kings on opposite sides, both sides race with pawns. f3 makes your centre rock solid, then g4 and h4-h5 go for Black's king.

lines.title: The Englund Gambit 1...e5
lines.intro: Three of your White games started 1.d4 e5. The gambit has one famous trap. Learn it once and you'll win many easy games.

moves.c: Take the pawn. The gambit is unsound.
Black attacks e5 and sets a trap.

quiz.q: Why not 4.Bf4 defending e5?
options: Because of 4...Qb4+ attacking both b2 and the bishop, a well-known trap
Because Bf4 blocks the f-pawn
Because the bishop is needed on c1
quiz.explain: After 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Bc3?? Bb4! Black wins. 4.Nc3 just develops and keeps a solid extra pawn.

moves.c: Now Bf4 is safe and hits the e5 knight.
The queen joins the attack on e5. White is a pawn up and better developed.

ideas.title: After the opening: what's the plan?
ideas.intro: You reach good positions from this opening, then lose the thread. Each position below comes from the lines you just learned. Find the move that fits the plan.

items.prompt: Black's bishop has just gone to e7. How do you use your lead in development?
items.explain: Take on c5. Black has to move the bishop again to win the pawn back, and you gain time for e4.

items.prompt: You're ahead in development. Open the centre.
items.explain: e4 opens lines while Black's king is still in the middle. If ...dxe4, Nxe4 hits the c5 bishop.

items.prompt: Kings on opposite sides. Which move starts your attack by trading Black's key defender?
items.explain: Bh6 trades off the g7 bishop, the piece that guards Black's king. Then f3, g4 and h4-h5.

items.prompt: Black checks you. What's the cleanest answer?
items.explain: c3 blocks the check with a pawn and keeps your knight on b5 aiming at c7. Blocking with a pawn is often better than moving the king or walking into a pin.

items.prompt: Black's d5 pawn looks protected by the queen. Is it really?
items.explain: 7.Qxd5 wins a pawn because 7...Qxd5 8.Nc7+ forks king and queen.

title: Caro-Kann Defence
sub: 1.e4 c6: your main defence as Black
why: You played the Caro-Kann in 47 games and score 54% with it. Most of your opponents play the Exchange line or 2.Nf3. This course covers everything you actually meet, plus the main lines you'll face as you get stronger.

lines.title: Exchange line: 3.exd5 cxd5
lines.intro: Your most common opponent choice. The position is symmetrical; your plan is quick development and ...Bg4 or ...Bf5 before playing ...e6.

moves.c: White aims the bishop at h7 and stops your ...Bf5.
Develop the light-squared bishop before ...e6 shuts it in. This is the whole point of the Caro-Kann.
Attacking b7.

quiz.q: Why is ...Qd7 fine here, even though b7 looks loose?
options: If Qxb7, then ...Rb8 chases the queen and Black wins the b2 pawn back with an active rook
b7 is defended by the bishop
White can't take because of check
quiz.explain: After Qxb7 Rb8 Qa6 Rxb2 Black's rook is on White's second rank. Greedy pawn grabs with the queen often go wrong.

moves.c: Equal. Plan: ...Rab8 and ...b5-b4 (the minority attack) to weaken White's queenside.

lines.title: Exchange with 4.Nf3 and Bb5
lines.intro: Several of your opponents play Nf3 and Bb5, pinning your knight. Stay calm, develop, and know one trick.

moves.c: Pinning the knight. It isn't a real threat yet.

quiz.q: If White now castles with 7.O-O, what do you play?
options: 7...Nxe5, and after 8.dxe5 Bxb5 you win a piece
7...e6, just developing
7...Qb6, attacking b2
quiz.explain: After ...Nxe5 dxe5 your d7 bishop takes the undefended b5 bishop. Black wins a whole piece. Players at your level fall for this all the time.

moves.c: White's best: take the bishop first.
Fully developed and equal. Later: ...O-O, ...Rac8 and ...a6 to ask the bishop a question.

lines.title: Advance: 3.e5 Bf5
lines.intro: White grabs space. You develop the bishop outside the pawn chain, then attack White's centre with ...c5.

moves.c: Bishop out before ...e6.

quiz.q: Why ...c5 now?
options: It attacks the d4 pawn, the base of White's pawn chain
It opens the diagonal for the queen
It prepares ...c4 to trap the bishop
quiz.explain: Attack the chain at its base. If d4 falls, e5 is weak too.

moves.c: Heading for f5 via g6 or c6-f5 ideas.
The knight goes to b6, eyeing c4, while the other knight blocks. Solid and active.

lines.title: Advance with 4.Bd3
lines.intro: Two of your opponents played 4.Bd3, offering to trade bishops. Take it: White's attacking bishop disappears and the queen is pulled out.

moves.c: Hit the base of the chain first.
A useful quiet move: it prepares ...c4 and ...b5, and keeps White's pieces out of b5. Next: ...Nge7-f5 and ...Qb6.

lines.title: 2.Nf3 d5 3.e5 Bg4
lines.intro: After 2.Nf3 and 3.e5 you can pin the knight with ...Bg4.

moves.c: Plan: ...Nf5, ...Qb6 and pressure on d4.
Solid, with pressure on d4.

lines.title: Classical: 3.Nc3 dxe4
lines.intro: The main line of the Caro-Kann. Know one trap here: never play ...Ngf6 when White's queen is on e2 and ...Nd7 blocks your king (Nd6 mate!).

moves.c: Make room so the bishop can go back to h7.
Solid. Castle short, then ...c5 or ...Qc7 and ...O-O-O. Black has no weaknesses.

lines.title: Panov Attack: 4.c4
lines.intro: White gets an isolated pawn on d4. You blockade it, trade pieces, and the endgame favours you.

quiz.q: What is Black's long-term plan here?
options: Blockade the d4 pawn with a piece on d5 and trade pieces towards an endgame
Attack the white king with ...g5
Win the d4 pawn right now with ...Qxd4
quiz.explain: An isolated pawn is strong in the middlegame and weak in the endgame. Put a piece on d5 in front of it and swap pieces.

moves.c: Your plan: ...Bb7, ...Rc8 and a knight to d5. Every trade brings you closer to an endgame where d4 is weak.

lines.title: 2.Bc4 lines
lines.intro: Three of your opponents played 2.Bc4. Just take the centre with ...d5.

moves.c: Pin, and pressure d4.
Comfortable. You have the Caro-Kann structure with your bishop outside the pawns.

ideas.title: Caro-Kann plans
ideas.intro: Typical moments from your Caro-Kann games. Find the plan move.

items.prompt: Classic Advance position. Strike at White's centre.
items.explain: ...c5 hits the d4 pawn, the base of White's chain. It's the standard break in the Advance.

items.prompt: Before you play ...e6, which piece should come out?
items.explain: Get the light-squared bishop out before ...e6 locks it in. That's the Caro-Kann's big idea.

items.prompt: White offers a bishop trade. What do you do?
items.explain: Take it. The bishop trade removes White's attacking bishop and pulls the queen to d3.

title: King's Indian Set-up
why: Against everything except 1.e4 you set up with ...Nf6, ...g6 and ...Bg7. It's a fighting system, but you need to know which pawn break to aim for, or you'll just wait and get squeezed.

lines.title: Classical: 4.e4 with c4
lines.intro: The main line. Your key break is ...e5, and later ...f5 to attack on the kingside while White attacks on the queenside.

moves.c: The key break. Strike at the centre.
Now the pawn chains are locked. White plays on the queenside with c5, you play on the kingside with ...f5.
Make room for the f-pawn.

quiz.q: What is the plan after ...f5?
options: ...f4, ...g5-g4 and a pawn storm against White's king
Trade queens and play an endgame
Play ...c5 and attack the queenside
quiz.explain: When the centre is locked, attack where your pawns point. Your pawns point at the kingside.

lines.title: Against the London (2.Bf4)
lines.intro: Against the London, don't wait. Hit back with ...c5 and ...Qb6 on the b2 pawn.

moves.c: The best reaction: pressure on d4.

quiz.q: What does ...Qb6 attack?
options: The b2 pawn, and it adds pressure to d4
The f2 pawn
The bishop on f4
quiz.explain: The London's weak point is b2 once the bishop leaves c1. ...Qb6 hits it.

moves.c: Harmonious. Black is fine.

lines.title: Against 2.Nc3 and 3.e4
lines.intro: When White plays e4 without c4, you get a Pirc-style position. Castle, then strike with ...c6 and ...e5.

moves.c: Your usual move. The engine slightly prefers 2...d5, because now White can grab the centre with e4. Your set-up is still fully playable.
Prepare ...e5.
The central break. Now your pieces come to life.

lines.title: Against Nf3 and g3
lines.intro: White fianchettoes too. Keep it simple: castle, then ...d6, ...Nc6 and ...e5.

quiz.q: Why ...a6 here?
options: Prepares ...Rb8 and ...b5, attacking White's c4 pawn
Stops Nb5 forever
Prepares ...Qa7
quiz.explain: This is the Panno plan: ...a6, ...Rb8, ...b5 hits c4 and opens lines on the queenside.

moves.c: Pressure on c4 and space on the queenside.

ideas.title: King's Indian plans
ideas.intro: Know your pawn breaks. These are the moments that decide KID games.

items.prompt: Classical position. What's your key central break?
items.explain: ...e5 strikes at the centre. Without it Black just gets squeezed.

items.prompt: Against the London, which pawn move gives you the most activity?
items.explain: ...c5 hits d4 and opens the way for ...Qb6 against b2.

items.prompt: Centre locked. Start your kingside attack.
items.explain: ...f5 is the standard King's Indian break once the centre is closed.

title: 1.e4 Repertoire
sub: The Ruy Lopez and your answers to 1...c5, 1...e6, 1...c6, 1...d5 and 1...d6
why: You play 1.e4 in about 40% of your White games: 3.Bb5 against 1...e5 and an early Nf3 against everything else. This course keeps your style (quick development, Nf3, Bb5) and fixes the lines where you drifted into passive positions.

lines.title: Ruy Lopez: main line
lines.intro: The Spanish. Pressure on the knight that defends e5, then a slow build-up with c3, d4 and a knight manoeuvre to g3.

moves.c: Attack the defender of e5.
Keep the pin-like pressure. 4.Bxc6 is fine too, but the main line keeps more tension.

quiz.q: Is the e4 pawn hanging after 5.O-O?
options: Not really: if 5...Nxe4, 6.Re1 or 6.d4 wins it back with a strong position
Yes, White just loses a pawn
Yes, so 5.d3 is forced
quiz.explain: Castling first is the main line. After ...Nxe4, the e-file opens against Black's king and White regains the pawn.

moves.c: Prepares d4 and gives the bishop a retreat to c2.
Stops ...Bg4 pinning your knight. Plan: d4, Nbd2-f1-g3, and a kingside attack.

lines.title: Ruy Lopez: 3...Bc5
lines.intro: A classical reply you've met. Use c3 and d4 to hit the bishop, then grab the e5 pawn.

moves.c: Prepares d4 with tempo on the bishop.
Straight into the centre.

quiz.q: Is it safe to take on e5?
options: Yes: after 6...Nxe5 7.dxe5 the knight on f6 is attacked and White keeps an extra central pawn
No, it loses the knight
Only after castling
quiz.explain: 6.Nxe5 wins a central pawn. Black's knight on f6 has to move and your e5 pawn cramps Black.

moves.c: Hits the knight and g7 at the same time. White is clearly better.

lines.title: Sicilian: the Rossolimo 3.Bb5
lines.intro: Against 1...c5 2...Nc6, put the bishop on b5 instead of c4. It develops quickly and often doubles Black's pawns.

moves.c: The Rossolimo. You avoid the huge Open Sicilian theory.
Give up the bishop to double Black's pawns.

quiz.q: What is White's plan here?
options: Bh6 to trade Black's strong bishop, and later f4 or a queenside squeeze against the doubled pawns
Castle queenside and push g4 at once
Play d4 immediately
quiz.explain: Trading the dark-squared bishops leaves Black's king and doubled c-pawns weak.

lines.title: French: the Exchange with Nf3
lines.intro: You like 3.exd5 against the French. Fine: the position is symmetrical, so develop fast and watch for a classic sacrifice on h7.

moves.c: Develop, aiming at h7.
Take the open e-file first.
A natural move, but a mistake.

quiz.q: Why does the sacrifice on h7 work here?
options: After Kxh7 Ng5+ your queen on d1 attacks the loose bishop on g4, so you win the piece back plus a pawn
It leads to a forced mate
It opens the h-file for your rook
quiz.explain: The "Greek gift": Bxh7+ Kxh7 Ng5+ uncovers your queen against g4. Always check what your pieces attack after a knight moves away.

moves.c: White is a clean pawn up and Black's king has lost its shelter.

lines.title: Caro-Kann: your 2.Nf3 line
lines.intro: You face the Caro-Kann yourself as Black, and as White you like 2.Nf3 and exd5. Here is the version that keeps an edge, with the trick you know from the Black side.

moves.c: Pin the knight.

quiz.q: Why 7.Nxd7 and not 7.O-O?
options: After 7.O-O?? Nxe5 8.dxe5 Bxb5 Black wins a piece
Nxd7 wins material
O-O is illegal here
quiz.explain: Exactly the trick from your Caro-Kann course, now from the other side: take on d7 first.

moves.c: Develop with pressure. Comfortable for White.

lines.title: Scandinavian: 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3
lines.intro: Take on d5 and develop with tempo on the queen.

moves.c: Develop and hit the queen.
Unpins the knight: now Nd5 and Nb5 tricks become possible.
Plan: O-O-O and a quick attack; Black's queen on a5 can become a target.

lines.title: Pirc and Modern: the 150 Attack
lines.intro: Against ...d6 and ...g6, set up Be3, Qd2 and O-O-O, then Bh6 and h4-h5. It's simple and dangerous.

moves.c: Aim for Qd2 and Bh6.

quiz.q: What's the next step of the plan?
options: Bh6 to trade Black's g7 bishop, then h4-h5
Retreat Be3 to e2
Play for d5 and a queenside attack
quiz.explain: The "150 Attack": trade the king's bishop, then open the h-file.

moves.c: Trade the key defender.

title: Italian Game
sub: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4: a simple, classical way to play 1.e4
why: You also play 1.e4 in about 40% of your White games, with Bb5 or Bc4. The Italian is the easiest 1.e4 opening to play well at your level: quick development, clear plans, and lots of traps for your opponents. It pairs well with the tactics you need to practise.

lines.title: Main line: 4.c3 and 5.d3
lines.intro: The modern Italian. Slow build-up: c3, d3, castle, then Re1, Nbd2-f1-g3 and a kingside attack.

moves.c: Aims at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
Prepares d4 later and gives the bishop a safe retreat square on b3.
Solid. Protects e4.
Keeps your bishop safe from ...b5.
Stops ...Bg4 and ...Ng4.

quiz.q: Where is this knight going?
options: g3, and then f5 or h5, to attack Black's king
e3, to control d5 only
back to d2
quiz.explain: The Nbd2-f1-g3 manoeuvre is the heart of the Italian. From g3 the knight jumps to f5.

moves.c: Next: d4 or Nh4-f5.

lines.title: Two Knights: 3...Nf6
lines.intro: Black attacks e4. The calm answer 4.d3 keeps everything solid and transposes to Italian set-ups.

moves.c: Hunting your bishop.

quiz.q: Why Bb5 instead of Bb3?
options: From b5 the bishop can't be trapped by ...c6 and ...b5, and it gives a check-free retreat to a4
To take on c6 immediately
Because b3 is controlled by the knight
quiz.explain: The knight on a5 would take on b3. Bb5 keeps the bishop, and ...a6 Ba4 ...b5 Bc2 is a well-known route.

moves.c: The standard Italian/Ruy structure. Plan: Nf1-g3, d4.

lines.title: Against 2...d6 (Philidor)
lines.intro: Two of your opponents played 2...d6. Hit the centre with 3.d4 and watch out for a nice trap.

moves.c: Grab the centre.

quiz.q: After 5.Qxf3 dxe5 6.Bc4, what is White threatening?
options: Qxf7 mate
Qb3 only
Bxf7+ winning a rook
quiz.explain: 6.Bc4 threatens Qxf7#. Black must play ...Qf6 or ...Nf6, and then Qb3 hits both b7 and f7.

moves.c: Double attack on b7 and f7.
White wins a pawn and Black's queenside is in chaos.

lines.title: The 3...Nd4 trap
lines.intro: Some players try 3...Nd4 hoping you grab e5. Don't!

quiz.q: What's wrong with 4.Nxe5?
options: 4...Qg5! attacks the e5 knight and g2 at once
Nothing, it wins a pawn
It loses the bishop on c4
quiz.explain: After 4.Nxe5? Qg5 White is in trouble, and 5.Nxf7?? Qxg2 is a disaster. Keep it simple.

moves.c: Trade it off.
Just castle. Black's pawn on d4 is weak and cut off, and you're ahead in development.
Put the rook behind your e-pawn. Next comes e5 to chase the knight, and Black's king is still in the centre.

title: Slav Defence
sub: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6: the Caro-Kann's twin against 1.d4
why: Against 1.d4 you play the King's Indian, which needs a lot of theory and sharp play. Because you already play the Caro-Kann, the Slav is a natural second option: same ...c6 and ...d5 ideas, same "bishop out first" rule, same kind of positions. Learn it if you ever want a quieter option against 1.d4.

lines.title: Main line: 4...dxc4 5.a4 Bf5
lines.intro: The classical main line. You take c4, then develop the bishop to f5 before ...e6.

moves.c: Grab the pawn. You won't keep it forever, but you gain time.
Stops ...b5.
Bishop out first, exactly like the Caro-Kann.
Pins the knight and controls e4.
Solid and equal. Plan: ...Qa5, ...e5 or ...c5 to free your game.

lines.title: 4.e3 Bf5
lines.intro: White protects c4 first. Get the bishop out.

moves.c: White hunts the bishop.

quiz.q: What happens after 7.Nxg6?
options: ...hxg6, and your h-file is open, which is fine for Black
Black loses a pawn
Black must recapture with the f-pawn
quiz.explain: ...hxg6 gives you a half-open h-file. This structure is known to be very solid.

moves.c: Normal development. Your h-file can be useful later.

lines.title: Exchange: 3.cxd5
lines.intro: A symmetrical structure. Just develop, and be careful about checks and pins.

moves.c: Counter-attack. Don't defend b7 passively.
Both sides have developed and the position is equal. Plan: ...Rc8, ...Qa5 and pressure down the c-file.

lines.title: Against the London
lines.intro: The London can be met with a Slav set-up too. The ...Qb6 idea works here as well.

moves.c: Hit the centre at once.

quiz.q: Why is ...Qb6 so effective against the London?
options: The bishop left c1, so b2 is undefended
It prepares ...Qxf2 mate
It defends d5
quiz.explain: Once the bishop goes to f4, b2 has no defender. ...Qb6 exploits that at once.

moves.c: Develop the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6. Comfortable for Black.
